title: Are You Boring Your Students Into Misbehavior?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that boredom is a direct and predictable cause of misbehavior, since students are naturally drawn to adventure, laughter, challenge, and fascination outside of school and will seek those same experiences inside the classroom if lessons fail to provide them. He organizes the piece around four student desires teachers should deliberately tap into: adventure, through scavenger hunts, dramatized read-alouds, and reenacted history; laughter, using humor to build rapport and reduce misbehavior; challenge, through open-ended, provocative questioning pitched just beyond what students are sure they can do; and fascination, by finding and amplifying the single most compelling detail within any lesson. He closes urging teachers to teach to students' hearts rather than simply deliver curriculum.
points: Treat student boredom as a predictable cause of misbehavior, not a personal failing of the students.
Build in adventure through scavenger hunts, dramatized read-alouds, or reenacted history.
Use humor deliberately - it builds rapport and reduces the likelihood of misbehavior.
Issue open-ended, provocative challenges pitched just beyond what students are sure they can do.
Find and amplify the single most fascinating detail in any lesson to hook attention.
quotes: And, as predictable as the rising sun, unengaged students misbehave, break rules, and seek fulfillment in less-than-acceptable ways.

Dive headlong into the dramatic stories of adventure behind the yawn-inducing curriculum you’ve been saddled with. Be wary of the current push in more and more technology, and get your students up and experiencing their learning.
The truth is, when your students are happy to be in your class, when they can have a good laugh once in a while, they’re less likely to misbehave and more open to learning.
Your job is to know what your students can do so you can ask for a little more—in tempting challenges dangled before them throughout the day.
Find the one thing that stands out and then make it compelling. Make it something your students can’t ignore, even if they tried.
